n0001.title: Writes and Write-Nots
n0001.gist: AI has removed the pressure that once forced everyone to learn to write, and this will split humanity into a shrinking group of clear thinkers and a growing group of write-nots.

n0002.title: The Coming Divide
n0002.gist: Paul Graham predicts that within a couple of decades most people will lose the ability to write well.

n0003.title: Article Metadata
n0003.gist: The post is dated October 2024 and framed as a short read.

n0005.navLabel: The post is framed as a short, three-minute read

n0008.title: A Bold Prediction
n0008.gist: The author predicts that within a couple of decades few people will still be able to write.

n0009.navLabel: The author predicts few people will be able to write within a couple decades

n0010.title: Why Writing Is So Hard
n0010.gist: Writing is difficult because it requires clear thinking, yet many jobs demand it, creating pressure that once forced people to buy, steal, or truly learn to write.

n0011.title: The Difficulty of Writing
n0011.gist: Writing is hard because it forces clear thinking, a struggle common even among capable people.

n0012.navLabel: Writers uniquely know how many people struggle with writing

n0013.navLabel: Writing is fundamentally difficult because it requires clear thinking

n0014.title: Writing Under Pressure
n0014.gist: Prestigious jobs often demand writing, and this pressure has driven even eminent professionals to plagiarize trivial passages.

n0015.navLabel: The most prestigious jobs tend to demand the most writing

n0016.navLabel: Pressure from writing expectations drives eminent professors to plagiarize petty boilerplate

n0017.title: Historical Escape Valves
n0017.gist: Before AI, those who couldn't write well had to pay someone else or plagiarize, so nearly everyone else had to learn to write.

n0018.navLabel: Before AI, only paying or plagiarizing let people avoid learning to write themselves

n0019.title: AI and the New Divide
n0019.gist: AI has eliminated the old pressure to write, splitting people into 'writes' and 'write-nots,' which the author argues is really a divide between thinkers and non-thinkers.

n0020.title: AI Removes the Pressure
n0020.gist: AI can now do the writing for people at school and work, dissolving the old incentive to learn.

n0021.navLabel: AI has dissipated nearly all pressure to learn writing at school and work

n0022.title: Writes vs Write-Nots
n0022.gist: The middle ground of merely adequate writers will vanish, leaving only good writers and non-writers.

n0023.navLabel: The ok-writer middle ground vanishes, leaving only good writers and write-nots

n0024.title: Is That So Bad
n0024.gist: One might object that this is just another skill made obsolete by technology, like blacksmithing.

n0025.navLabel: One might compare this obsolescence to blacksmithing's harmless disappearance

n0026.title: Writing Is Thinking
n0026.gist: The author insists this loss matters because writing is itself a form of thinking, as Leslie Lamport's quote captures.

n0027.navLabel: Writing is thinking, echoing Leslie Lamport's point about a unique kind of thought

n0028.navLabel: If you're thinking without writing, you only think you're thinking

n0029.title: A World of Think-Nots
n0029.gist: The write-not divide is really a think-not divide, and the author is clear about which side he wants to be on.

n0030.navLabel: The writes/write-nots divide is really a thinks/think-nots divide, and the author picks a side

n0031.title: Consequences and Conclusion
n0031.gist: Just as industrialization made physical strength optional, technology will make clear thinking through writing a matter of choice.

n0032.title: The Strength Analogy
n0032.gist: As physical labor's decline let people choose to be strong through exercise, technology will let people choose to be smart through writing.

n0033.navLabel: Preindustrial strength became a choice once physical labor declined, via exercise

n0034.navLabel: Smartness through writing will likewise become something only some choose to pursue
